id: A Song of a Young Lady to Her Ancient Lover

### The Vow of Devotion

Let the clamor of younger suitors fall away unheard; their fleeting, callow passion holds no allure for a heart that has made its ultimate choice. Turning her back entirely on the eager pursuits of youth, the speaker resolves to remain solely and unreservedly devoted to her elderly lover. Where others might see only the evening of life, she recognizes a profound depth born of time and experience—a rich landscape that no inexperienced youth could ever match. Her fidelity is absolute, bound to a singular devotion that rejects the superficial clamor of the world.

In their quiet intimacy, she seeks to defy the encroaching chill of the years. Through her passionate kisses, she vows to breathe new warmth into his spirit, effectively bridging the divide between her youth and his fading vitality. Her lips become a conduit of life and tenderness, intent on melting the frost of passing time and reigniting the embers of his youthful spirit. With every embrace, she aims to remind him that passion is not the exclusive domain of the young, but a flame that can be rekindled at any stage of life.

Her devotion extends beyond gentle gestures into a deliberate effort to soften the physical burdens of aging. Through her soothing and intentional touch, she promises to ease his weariness, soothing aching limbs and reassuring his fragile frame. She uses her hands to trace the lines carved by time, treating his body not as a vessel in decay, but as a masterpiece deserving of reverence. In doing so, she endeavors to restore his lost vigor, coaxing strength back into his step and warmth into his blood.

This act of love is both a heartfelt impulse and a refined art. Pledging to employ both her intuitive skill and deep emotional affection, she dedicates herself to maximizing her partner’s pleasure and delight. Every movement is tailored to his needs, driven by a desire to ensure that his senses remain vibrant and alive. She seeks to surround him with a sanctuary of joy, proving that intimacy, when fueled by true devotion, can unlock new depths of bliss regardless of age.

Ultimately, her vow stands firm against the natural course of human frailty. Her love is neither conditional nor temporary; it does not waver in the face of physical decline. Instead, she offers an enduring, sincere affection that transcends the superficialities of youth and smooth skin. In her eyes, his aging form remains a treasure, and her commitment remains an unshakable haven—a timeless love that shines all the brighter as the daylight fades.
outputs.L4:
I look at you now, across the quiet sanctuary of our room where the evening shadows stretch long, and I see the relentless march of time etched upon your face. The silver in your hair was bought with decades of devotion; the quiet fatigue in your shoulders speaks of a body weary from the long climb of life. The hands that once lifted heavy burdens and held me with effortless strength now rest in your lap, pale and trembling, cooled by the encroaching winter of age. I know you feel the loss of your youth—a quiet sorrow for the vibrant, untamed vigor that once defined you. 

To me, however, you are not a fading shadow. I refuse to let the frost of elderhood settle over your heart. 

I step across the floor and kneel before your chair, closing the distance that time has tried to carve between us. Taking your hands in mine, frail and cold, I press them against my cheek, breathing my own body’s heat into your worn skin. I lean in close, offering no grand declarations, only the gentle, persistent melody of my presence. 

I press a soft kiss to your furrowed brow, smoothing away the tension of a thousand worries. I kiss your closed eyelids, honoring the long years of sight that have witnessed both joy and sorrow. And then, leaning closer still, I meet your lips with a tender, unhurried kiss—a devotion forged in the fire of everything we have weathered together. My touch is deliberate and soft, tracing the line of your jaw, whispering without words that you are still desired, still cherished, and deeply needed.

And slowly, miraculously, the tide begins to turn. 

Beneath my fingertips, I feel a sudden, quickened pulse. A soft breath escapes your lips, carrying with it the cold weight of your weariness. As my mouth lingers against yours, a wave of familiar warmth rushes back into your skin. Your eyes open, no longer clouded by the gray mist of exhaustion, but glowing with an amber spark I haven't seen in years. Your arms, once hesitant, rise to encircle me, pulling me close with a strength that defies the frailty of flesh.

In that breathless moment, your former vitality ignites once more. It is not the superficial beauty of youth, but something far grander: the fierce, enduring passion of a soul awakened by love. 

Let the world believe that passion belongs only to the young. Here, in the shelter of our embrace, we know the truth. Age may soften the body and slow the stride, but genuine love possesses a sacred power—a devotion so steadfast that it can breathe heat into cold hearths, call back lost vigor, and shine triumphantly against the fading light.

counterfactuals.output:
Here is the full text of the poem **"A Song"** (sometimes titled *"To an Ancient Person"*) by John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester:

***

Ancient person, for whom I
All the flattering skills on earth
Have employed, and yet can find
Nothing equal to your worth;

Will you turn your eyes and see
What a wretched wretch I am?
Pale, and weeping, and for thee
Dying of a painful flame.

Kindness has resistless charms;
All besides but weakly move;
Fiercest anger it disarms,
And repays the griefs of love.

Love does other passions kill;
Kindness does love's self subdue;
You may make me what you will,
Do but make me happy too.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
Let senseless nymphs for boyish lovers sigh,
Whose shallow passions blossom, fade, and die;
Give me the oak that braved the tempest’s rage,
Dignified by time, august with noble age!
Though silver frost upon thy temples lies,
A bright, immortal flame illumes thine eyes.

So Cytherea sought the sacred grove,
And chose Anchises for her monarch love;
She scorned the striplings of the Olympian court,
For grander pleasures and a richer sport.
Thy honored brow bears majesty and grace,
Which fleeting years may touch, but ne'er deface.

Am I not young? Is not my bosom sweet?
Does not my heart with furious passion beat?
Then let my kisses all thy chills destroy,
And wake thy sleeping blood to warmth and joy!
My eager lips shall press thy frosty brow,
And teach thy languid veins new life to know.

Like golden ivy round the ancient tree,
My youth shall weave its tender life round thee.
My panting sighs shall lend thee vital breath,
And snatch thy spirits from the chill of death;
Each warm embrace shall melt the winter snows,
Till in thy breast a second summer glows!

Yield, noble Lord, to Love’s reviving art,
And drink the fire from my boundless heart.
We’ll mock the glass of Time, and boldly prove,
That Age is vanquished by the Power of Love!

counterfactuals.output:
"**Ancient Person of My Heart**" (usually titled simply "**Song**" or known by its first line) is a Restoration-era poem written by **John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester** (1647–1680). 

Here are the complete lyrics/lines to the poem:

***

Ancient person, for whom I
All the flattering youth defy,
Long be it ere thou grow old,
Aching, cowering, and cold;
Not but that thy sweet eyes shine
When thy youth is past, like mine,
And thy love continue still,
When thy power to please shall fail.

Tie me to thee by thy charms,
There indulge me in thy arms;
For thy past kindness, slake thy lust,
And be faithful to my dust.

***

### Context & Meaning:
* **The Speaker:** The poem features a speaker addressing an older lover ("ancient person"), rejecting younger, more conventional suitors in favor of someone mature.
* **Themes:** Typical of Rochester’s witty and cynical Restoration poetry, it blends sincere affection with a pragmatic, unromantic acceptance of aging, mortality, and physical decay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
Here is the text for John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester's poem, **"A Song to an Ancient Person of Quality."**

***

### A Song to an Ancient Person of Quality

Ancient person, for whom I
All the flattering hopes defy
Of frail beauty’s charms, and try
Whether youth be worth a sigh:

Thou, for whom I only grieve
I should lose the power to give
To deceive, and be deceived,
For the things that youth can give:

Who, when age has lost the power,
Canst go on to love the more;
And in spite of old decay,
Keep’st alive the pleasing May.

Love thy virtue does restore,
Which youth spoiled with lust before;
Making thee appear more bright
In thy evening than thy light.

***

### Brief Context for Your Research
Written in the 1670s, this poem is a classic example of Rochester subverting traditional Restoration love poetry conventions. Rather than praising a young, fleetingly beautiful maiden (a standard trope of the era), the speaker addresses an older woman, arguing that mature love—purified of youthful lust and deceit—is far more constant, virtuous, and enduring.
